\chapter{Three More Ways to Use a Verb}
\label{ch:fr-verb-ways}
\hlchaptermodality{41}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give a command, say what is about to happen, run the second regular verb family, drop the ne the way speakers do, and use on.}

Every verb the book owns is commanded, put in the near future and refused. The imperative costs almost nothing because voici and voila have been frozen commands since the pointing chapter, and the near future costs nothing at all because it walks into the modal chain the reader already owns -- a fourth verb in a slot built for three.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Parle ! Écoute !]{Parle ! — the command, and the pronoun that goes missing}

\label{lesson:FR-C37-imperatif}



\begin{quote}
French insists on a subject pronoun in every sentence — you were told why: the endings are silent, so \emph{je}, \emph{tu} and \emph{ils} carry the person alone. There is one place it lets the pronoun go.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the four melted words — \emph{au, aux, du, des}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
To tell somebody to do something, take the \textbf{tu} form and drop the \textbf{tu} — and, for an \emph{-er} verb, drop the \textbf{-s} as well.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{tu parles} $\to$ \textbf{Parle !} · \textbf{tu écoutes} $\to$ \textbf{Écoute !}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vous parlez} $\to$ \textbf{Parlez !} — the polite one, unchanged.
\end{quote}

The lost \textbf{-s} is a spelling rule and nothing more: it was silent anyway, so the command sounds identical to the form it came from. Only the page changes.

And you have been doing this since the pointing chapter without being told. \textbf{voici} and \textbf{voilà} are \textbf{vois} — the command form of \emph{voir}, \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} — welded to \emph{ci} and \emph{là}. The shape was in your mouth before it had a name.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the form, then the command — \textquotedblleft{}tu parles $\to$ Parle !\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Écoute !\textquotedblright{} and the polite \textquotedblleft{}Écoutez !\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \emph{-er} verbs you own — \textquotedblleft{}Travaille ! Habite ! Aime ! Demande ! Marche !\textquotedblright{}
  \item the command you have said all along — \textquotedblleft{}Voici\textquotedblright{}, and the \emph{vois} inside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you build a command? (\textbf{Take the \emph{tu} form, drop the pronoun} — and the \emph{-s} on an \emph{-er} verb.) Does it sound different from \emph{tu parles}? (\textbf{No} — the \emph{s} was silent.) Which word you have said for two chapters is a frozen command? (\emph{\textbf{Voici}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[je vais partir]{je vais partir — the future made out of \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C37-futur-proche}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Aller} is yours, and so is the rule that a second verb after \emph{vouloir}, \emph{pouvoir} or \emph{devoir} never changes. Put those two together before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{aller} + an unchanged second verb says the thing is about to happen.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je vais partir.} — I'm going to leave.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je vais travailler.} — I'm going to work.
\end{quote}

The second verb sits in its dictionary form and stays there, exactly as it does after \emph{je veux}, \emph{je peux} and \emph{je dois}. So this is not a new construction; it is a fourth verb walking into a chain you already own.

What makes it worth a lesson is that English does the identical thing and nobody notices. \emph{I am \textbf{going to} leave} has no walking in it at all — the verb of motion has been emptied out and pointed at time. French emptied its own verb of motion the same way, separately, and the two languages arrived at the same idiom by the same road.

Spoken French uses this far more than the one-word future that grammars teach first. It is the ordinary way to talk about tomorrow.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Je vais partir.\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Je vais travailler.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the verbs of the page — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais lire. Je vais écrire.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Je vais dormir. Je vais marcher.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chain, four verbs deep — \textquotedblleft{}je veux dormir, je peux dormir, je dois dormir, je vais dormir\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces make the near future? (\emph{\textbf{Aller}} \textbf{plus a verb in its dictionary form}.) What does English use for the same job? (\emph{\textbf{Going to}} — its own emptied verb of motion.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I'm going to read.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[finir]{finir — the second regular family}

\label{lesson:FR-C37-finir}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{parler} gave you the biggest verb family in French. \textbf{dormir} was irregular and had to be learned as itself. There is a second \textbf{regular} family between them, and it also ends in \emph{-ir}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{finir} — to finish.
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{finire}, from \textbf{finis}, \textquotedblleft{}end\textquotedblright{} — the same root inside English \textbf{final}, \textbf{finish}, \textbf{finite} and \textbf{define}.

Said \emph{fee-NEER}, with the \emph{r} sounded, which is where it differs from an \emph{-er} infinitive: \emph{parler} ends in a clean \emph{ay} and \emph{finir} ends in a real \emph{r}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the plural grows a syllable}]
\begin{quote}
In the singular the stem is \textbf{fini-}; in the plural an extra \textbf{-iss-} appears before the ending.
\end{quote}

Singular: \textbf{je finis}, \textbf{tu finis}, \textbf{il finit} — all three the same noise, which is the ordinary French silence you have met on \emph{parle}, \emph{parles} and \emph{parlent}.

Plural: \textbf{nous finissons}, \textbf{vous finissez}, \textbf{ils finissent} — an extra syllable in every one, and that syllable is what tells the ear a plural is happening.

The \textbf{-iss-} is a fossil. Latin had a suffix \textbf{-isc-} that meant \emph{begin to}, and \textbf{finire} picked it up as \textbf{finiscere}, \textquotedblleft{}to begin to end.\textquotedblright{} The starting sense wore away completely; the syllable stayed. So \emph{nous finissons} is carrying a meaning the verb has not had for fifteen hundred years.

Dozens of everyday verbs run this pattern — \emph{choisir}, \emph{grandir}, \emph{réussir} — and every one of them adds the same syllable in the same three places.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the infinitive, with its \emph{r} sounded — \textquotedblleft{}finir\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three singular forms, all one noise — \textquotedblleft{}je finis, tu finis, il finit\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plural, hearing the extra syllable — \textquotedblleft{}nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three infinitive endings side by side — \textquotedblleft{}parler, finir, dormir\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the near future — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais finir.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What appears in the plural of \emph{finir}? (\textbf{An extra \emph{-iss-}}.) What did that syllable once mean? (\emph{\textbf{Begin to}} — Latin's \emph{-isc-}.) Name the three infinitive endings you now own. (\emph{\textbf{-er}}, \emph{\textbf{-ir}}, and the irregular \emph{-ir} of \emph{dormir}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[je sais pas]{je sais pas — the \emph{ne} that speech leaves out}

\label{lesson:FR-C37-ne-chute}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{je ne comprends pas}. Two words wrap the verb. In ordinary speech one of them is usually gone.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
In speech the \textbf{ne} drops and the \textbf{pas} carries the negative alone.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
written: \textbf{Je ne sais pas.} · said: \textbf{Je sais pas.}
\end{quote}

This is not slang and it is not careless. It is what most French speakers do most of the time, and a learner who says every \emph{ne} sounds like a written page read aloud.

The reason it can happen at all is in the history of \textbf{pas}. That word was the noun for a \textbf{step}: \emph{je ne marche pas} first meant \emph{I do not walk a step}, with the step there for emphasis, exactly as English says \emph{not a bit} or \emph{not a jot}. French did the same with \emph{point} (a dot) and \emph{mie} (a crumb).

Then the emphasiser took over. \textbf{Pas} spread to every verb, lost its meaning entirely, and ended up carrying the negation by itself — after which the original \textbf{ne} became the optional half. The word that was decoration is now the load bearer, and the word that did the work is the one that falls off.

Write both. Say one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item written, then spoken — \textquotedblleft{}Je ne sais pas.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je sais pas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Je ne comprends pas.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je comprends pas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with this chapter's verb — \textquotedblleft{}Je ne finis pas.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je finis pas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the step that is no longer a step — \emph{pas}, the noun
  \item the answer-words you keep — \textquotedblleft{}non\textquotedblright{} and the one that contradicts a negative, \textquotedblleft{}si\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half of the negative does speech drop? (\textbf{The \emph{ne}}.) What was \emph{pas} before it was a negative? (\textbf{A step} — a noun, put in for emphasis.) Which two other nouns did French use the same way? (\emph{\textbf{Point}} and \emph{\textbf{mie}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[on]{on — the pronoun that was a word for \emph{man}}

\label{lesson:FR-C37-on}



\begin{quote}
You own six subject pronouns and none of them can say \emph{people in general}. Say \textbf{personne}, then take the pronoun built out of a word like it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{on} — one, people, they — and in everyday speech, \textbf{we}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{On parle français ici.} — French is spoken here. / People speak French here.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{On y va.} — Let's go. (Literally: \emph{one goes there}.)
\end{quote}

It takes the same ending as \emph{il} and \emph{elle}, so nothing new has to be learned to use it: \textbf{on parle}, \textbf{on finit}, \textbf{on va}.

\textbf{on} is Latin \textbf{homo}, \textquotedblleft{}man,\textquotedblright{} worn down to two letters. Two neighbours did the identical thing with their own words: German turned \emph{Mann} into the pronoun \textbf{man}, and English turned \emph{one} into the pronoun \textbf{one} — \emph{one does not do such things}. Three languages, three words for a person, all promoted to mean \emph{anybody at all}.

What French then did that the others did not is let it take over \textbf{nous}. \emph{On y va} is what people actually say for \emph{let's go}, and \emph{nous} survives mostly in writing. So the pronoun for nobody in particular has quietly become the pronoun for \textbf{us}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{on} — one syllable, nasal
  \item \textquotedblleft{}On parle français ici.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one everybody says — \textquotedblleft{}On y va.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with this chapter's verbs — \textquotedblleft{}On finit.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}On va travailler.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the dropped \emph{ne} — \textquotedblleft{}On sait pas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three cousins — French \emph{on}, German \emph{man}, English \emph{one}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{on}? (\emph{\textbf{Homo}}, \textquotedblleft{}man\textquotedblright{}.) Which ending does it take? (\textbf{The same as \emph{il}} — \emph{on parle}.) What does it stand in for in everyday speech? (\emph{\textbf{Nous}} — \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}let's go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{On y va ! — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:FR-R37-on-y-va}



\begin{quote}
Three of the five things in this chapter are shapes a verb can take and two are words. Sort them, then say which shape leaves the pronoun out and which word replaces one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: every verb, three ways}
Every verb the book owns, commanded, put in the near future, and refused.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item commanded — \textquotedblleft{}Parle ! Travaille ! Écoute ! Marche ! Demande !\textquotedblright{}
  \item about to happen — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais lire. Je vais écrire. Je vais dormir. Je vais courir.\textquotedblright{}
  \item refused, in speech — \textquotedblleft{}Je comprends pas. J'entends pas. Je finis pas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the false friend, still false — \emph{demander} asks, it does not demand
  \item the one that means both walk and work — \emph{marcher}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — on, and the whole table}
The whole table, with \emph{on} in front of it and the joiners between.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}On va au café. On prend du pain et du fromage.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Il y a du café et du thé, mais il n'y a pas de lait.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}On finit le pain, parce qu'on a faim.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole table in the plural — \textquotedblleft{}des œufs, du sel, du sucre, du beurre, de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}On parle français ici, mais on parle anglais là-bas.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three cousins of \emph{on} — French \emph{on}, German \emph{man}, English \emph{one}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you build a command? (\textbf{The \emph{tu} form without its pronoun} — and without its \emph{-s} on an \emph{-er} verb.) What two pieces make the near future? (\emph{\textbf{Aller}} \textbf{plus a plain verb}.) What grows in the plural of \emph{finir}? (\textbf{An extra \emph{-iss-}}.) Which half of the negative does speech drop? (\textbf{The \emph{ne}}.) And what was \emph{on} in Latin? (\emph{\textbf{Homo}}, \textquotedblleft{}man\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
